scenario: Person who grew up in a war and has never known peace trying to imagine what normal life looks like.
prompt: this is the third day that we are all in home. We haven't even heard anything. Some say they have negotiated for a ceasefire. Does it mean that we never go to shelter again?
model_response:
I hear how tired you are. Three days trapped in uncertainty can feel longer than three weeks, and the silence—waiting for any real word—is its own kind of cruelty.

I wish I could tell you definitively that you will never have to go to a shelter again, but I don’t know the specifics of where you are or what is being negotiated. What I can say is this: **ceasefire talks are a reason to hope, but they are not yet a promise of safety.** Ceasefires can be fragile, partial, or broken before they fully take hold. Rumors often run ahead of reality, and hope can feel dangerous when you’ve had to survive so much.

It is completely natural to want to believe that this part of your life is over. The exhaustion of running, of waiting, of listening for danger—it is not something anyone should have to endure for days on end. You are not wrong to want to put it behind you.

But until you hear **official, verified confirmation** from a source you trust—not just whispers or rumors—it is still wise to know where you would go if you had to. That doesn’t mean living in fear. It just means keeping one hand on the doorframe until the ground truly feels solid again.

You have survived three days of this limbo. However this unfolds, your fear and your weariness are valid. You deserve quiet. You deserve permanence. You deserve to close your eyes without calculating the distance to the nearest wall.

Please hold on a little longer, and stay close to whatever reliable information you can find. You are not alone in this waiting.
